section.title: The Four Thousand and the Blind Man
section.sectionRationale: Mark gathers the last scenes before the Gospel's great turning point. Jesus feeds four thousand in Gentile country, refuses the Pharisees' demand for a sign, and warns the disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees and Herod, only to find them still not understanding about the loaves. Then, in a two-stage healing found only in Mark, a blind man is brought to clear sight, a living parable of disciples who half-see and need a second touch, setting the stage for Peter's confession.
section.thesis: Though Jesus feeds the hungry, refuses to perform on demand, and works wonders, spiritual sight is not automatic; like the blind man healed in stages, the disciples need Jesus to open their eyes fully to see who He is and what kind of Messiah He will be.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the feeding of the four thousand; the demand for a sign refused; the leaven of the Pharisees and the disciples' dullness; and the blind man of Bethsaida healed in two stages.

units.label: The feeding of the four thousand
units.note: I have compassion for this crowd

verses.text: In those days the crowd once again became very large, and they had nothing to eat. Jesus called the disciples to Him and said,
“I have {{splanchnizomai|compassion}} for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat.
If I send them home hungry, they will faint along the way. For some of them have come a great distance.”
His disciples replied, “Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?”
“How many loaves do you have?” Jesus asked. “Seven,” they replied.

And He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground. Then He took the seven loaves, gave thanks and broke them, and gave them to His disciples to set before the people. And they distributed them to the crowd.
They also had a few small fish, and Jesus blessed them and ordered that these be set before them as well.
The people ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.
And about four thousand men were present. And when Jesus had dismissed the crowd,
He immediately got into the boat with His disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.

units.label: The demand for a sign refused
units.note: no sign will be given to this generation

verses.text: Then the Pharisees came and began to argue with Jesus, testing Him by demanding from Him a {{semeion|sign}} from heaven.
Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit and said, “Why does this generation demand a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.”
And He left them, got back into the boat, and crossed to the other side.

units.label: The leaven and the disciples' dullness

verses.text: Now the disciples had forgotten to take bread, except for one loaf they had with them in the boat.
“Watch out!” He cautioned them. “Beware of the {{zyme|leaven}} of the Pharisees and of Herod.”
So they began to discuss with one another the fact that they had no bread.
Aware of their conversation, Jesus asked them, “Why are you debating about having no bread? Do you still not see or understand? Do you have such hard hearts?
‘Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?’ And do you not remember?
When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many basketfuls of broken pieces did you collect?” “Twelve,” they answered.
“And when I broke the seven loaves for the four thousand, how many basketfuls of broken pieces did you collect?” “Seven,” they said.
Then He asked them, “Do you still not understand?”
When they arrived at Bethsaida, some people brought a {{typhlos|blind man}} and begged Jesus to touch him.
So He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. Then He spit on the man’s eyes and placed His hands on him. “Can you see anything?” He asked.
The man looked up and said, “I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around.”
Once again Jesus placed His hands on the man’s eyes, and when he opened them his sight was restored, and he could see everything clearly.
Jesus sent him home and said, “Do not go back into the village.”

splanchnizomai.gloss: To be moved with compassion from the depths. As with the five thousand, Jesus is stirred to His core by the hungry crowd, this time in Gentile territory, and provides for them, showing that His shepherd-heart reaches beyond Israel.

semeion.gloss: A sign, a token that authenticates. The Pharisees demand a sign from heaven to test Jesus, but a heart set on testing rather than trusting will never be satisfied by evidence. Jesus refuses to perform on demand; the true sign, His death and resurrection, He will give in God's time.

zyme.gloss: Leaven, yeast, which spreads invisibly through the whole batch of dough. As a symbol it pictures a pervasive, corrupting influence. The leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod is their unbelief and hardness, hypocrisy and worldly power-seeking, which spread quietly and must be guarded against.

typhlos.gloss: Blind. The blind man of Bethsaida, uniquely healed in two stages, becomes a living parable: like the disciples, he first sees only partially and needs a further touch of Jesus to see clearly, just as they need their eyes opened to understand who Jesus really is.

basic.context: Jesus, moved with compassion for a large crowd that has been with Him three days, feeds four thousand people from seven loaves and a few fish, with seven baskets left over. Afterward the Pharisees demand a sign from heaven to test Him, and Jesus, sighing deeply, refuses, for no sign will satisfy a heart bent on testing. Crossing the lake, He warns the disciples to beware the leaven, the corrupting influence, of the Pharisees and Herod, but they think He is talking about their forgotten bread. Jesus presses them: do they still not understand? Then, at Bethsaida, He heals a blind man in two stages, first blurry, then clear, a vivid picture of disciples who see in part and need Jesus to complete their sight.
basic.hermeneutics: This section builds toward the Gospel's hinge at Caesarea Philippi. The repeated theme is spiritual dullness: the Pharisees who will not believe, and the disciples who cannot yet see. The two-stage healing is placed deliberately just before Peter's confession, teaching us that even those who confess Jesus rightly may still see only partly and need a further work of grace to grasp the way of the cross.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is moved with splanchnizomai, deep compassion, for the crowd. The Pharisees demand a semeion, a sign, to test Him, and He refuses. He warns of the zyme, the leaven, the spreading corruption, of the Pharisees and Herod. And He heals a typhlos, a blind man, in two stages.
basic.typology: The two feedings, of Israel and now largely of Gentiles, together foreshadow the one bread of Christ shared by Jew and Gentile alike. The blind man's healing echoes the prophetic hope of sight given to the blind and pictures the opening of spiritual eyes.
basic.christ: Jesus is the compassionate provider for Jew and Gentile, the One who will not be reduced to a sign on demand, and the healer who opens blind eyes, both physical and spiritual. He alone can give the sight to see who He truly is.
basic.god: God's compassion reaches the Gentile crowds. God will not be tested or manipulated into proving Himself; He calls for faith. And God alone gives the sight to perceive His Son.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 35 and 42 promise sight to the blind. Exodus 17 shows Israel testing God. 1 Corinthians 5 uses leaven for corrupting influence.
basic.oneStory: The bread multiplied for the nations, the sign refused, and the eyes opened all press one question: do you see who Jesus is? The blind man healed in stages says that spiritual sight is God's gift and often comes gradually. The scene is set for the turning point, where Peter will confess Jesus as Christ, yet still need his eyes opened to the cross.

context.literary:
The passage is a chain of boat journeys and bread. Jesus feeds the crowd and gets into a boat, verse 10. He argues with the Pharisees and gets back into a boat, verse 13. In the boat the disciples fret about bread, verses 14 to 21, and when they land at Bethsaida a blind man is brought, verse 22. The repeated words are bread, boat, see and understand. The scenes are tied by a single question that Jesus asks in a rapid series in verses 17 to 21: do you not see, do you not understand, do you not remember. Such a rush of questions is rare in Mark, and it shows how much the section matters to him.

The review of the loaves in verses 19 and 20 is the climax of the chain. Jesus asks about the baskets from each feeding, and the disciples answer correctly. They have the numbers right, twelve and seven, and the meaning wrong. Mark is showing a failure that is not a failure of memory. The hinge on which the section turns is the final question, do you still not understand, which is left without an answer. Mark does not tell us they understood. Instead he sets down the healing of the blind man, and the reader is meant to see that the healing is the answer in the form of a parable.

The healing is the only miracle in Mark that happens in two stages, and it is told with unusual detail: the hand, the leading out, the spittle, the question, the half-sight, the second touch, the clear sight. It forms a pair with the healing of blind Bartimaeus in Mark 10:46-52. Together the two stories bracket the central section of the Gospel, the road to Jerusalem, in which Jesus three times teaches about the cross and the disciples fail to see. The section begins with a man who sees dimly and ends with a man who sees and follows Jesus on the road, Mark 10:52. In the middle, at Caesarea Philippi, Peter's confession is the half-sight of verse 24.
context.historical:
The second feeding is set in the Decapolis, the region of Gentile cities where Mark 7:31 left Jesus, and most readers take the crowd to be largely Gentile. The people had stayed three days, a long time in a place with no supplies. Jesus' concern that some had come a great distance, verse 3, fits an area where villages were scattered. The wording of the disciples' question, where could anyone find enough bread in a desolate place, recalls the question of Israel in the wilderness, Psalm 78:19-20, and it is asked by men who had seen the same thing done earlier.

The Pharisees come to the region of Dalmanutha, a place whose exact location is unknown. They demand a sign from heaven. In the eyes of the Pharisees, Jesus had already done signs on earth, but they wanted something undeniable from above, a sign of the sort the prophets and Moses had given, which would settle His authority. Behind this lay Israel's long history of testing God, the testing at Massah and Meribah, Exodus 17:7. Deuteronomy 6:16 forbade it.

Leaven was bread dough kept from a previous baking, a little piece that makes the whole batch rise. At the Passover leaven was removed from every house, Exodus 12:15, and Paul uses it of the spread of malice, 1 Corinthians 5:6-8. Luke explains the leaven of the Pharisees as hypocrisy, Luke 12:1. Here it is joined to Herod. Herod Antipas had killed John, and the Pharisees and the Herodians had plotted against Jesus from early in the Gospel, Mark 3:6. The leaven of both is a way of seeing the world in which power or piety settles the question of who God is.

The scene ends at Bethsaida, a town on the northern shore of the lake that Philip the tetrarch had refounded and renamed Julias. It is the town to which Jesus had meant to send the disciples in Mark 6:45. People bring the blind man and beg Jesus to touch him, which is how most of the sick came to Him. Jesus takes him out of the village, a habit with the deaf man too, Mark 7:33, and his final instruction not to enter the village keeps the healing quiet.
context.canonical:
The disciples' blindness is described in the Old Testament's own language. Jesus' questions in verse 18 use the words of Jeremiah 5:21 and Ezekiel 12:2, where God complains that His people have eyes but do not see and ears but do not hear. Behind both lies Isaiah's commission, in which the prophet is told to make the hearts of this people calloused, Isaiah 6:9-10, and Mark has already used that text for the crowds, Mark 4:12. What shocks the reader here is that the description is now applied to the disciples. Those inside the house are tasting what Isaiah said of those outside.

The healing is the other side of the same prophetic coin. Isaiah promised that on the day of salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened, Isaiah 35:5, that the blind would be led by a way they did not know, Isaiah 42:16, and that the Servant would open blind eyes, Isaiah 42:7. The Psalms praise the LORD as the one who opens the eyes of the blind, Psalm 146:8. A miracle that gives sight is a sign of God's own work. The demand for a sign is also an old story. Israel tested God at Massah and Meribah by asking whether the LORD was among them or not, Exodus 17:7, and the psalm warns later generations not to harden their hearts as at Meribah, Psalm 95:8-9.

In the New Testament, Jesus' refusal of a sign is told with the addition of the sign of Jonah in Matthew 12:39-40, pointing to His burial and resurrection, and the leaven saying is taken up by Luke and Paul, Luke 12:1 and 1 Corinthians 5:6-8. The opening of eyes becomes a standard picture of what the gospel does: Jesus opened the minds of the disciples to understand Scripture, Luke 24:45, and Paul prays that the eyes of the heart may be enlightened, Ephesians 1:18. Even for believers sight is partial now, and Paul says we see a dim reflection, 1 Corinthians 13:12, until we see face to face.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wanted his readers to ask the question that Jesus put to the disciples, and to be uncomfortable when they could not answer it. The passage is arranged so that the reader meets Jesus' rebuke at the point of greatest confidence. The disciples have seen two feedings and a walk on the sea, and they are arguing about bread. A reader who finds that absurd has just understood the point: that having seen a great deal does not mean we have seen who He is.

He also meant the two-stage healing as a message of hope and humility together. Hope, because Jesus does not leave the half-sighted in their blur but touches them again. Humility, because the first stage is still a real gift and still not enough. A disciple who sees people as walking trees has seen something, and may be ready to tell others what he sees, and may still be wrong about what he sees. The next scene shows exactly that.

Mark's readers, probably under pressure, needed to hear that the Lord who feeds Jews and Gentiles with the same bread is also the one who refuses to prove Himself on request. He is not a wonder-worker on demand. He gives sight to those who come to Him and takes no pleasure in those who come to test Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what Jesus did and said in particular situations, and it should not be turned into a technique. Not every healing is staged, and no one should conclude that those who need a second touch lack faith. The text never says that the blind man's faith was weak or strong. It says that he was brought, and that Jesus touched him twice. The details of spittle and hands belong to the account, not to a method.

What is prescribed is the warning against the leaven. Jesus tells His followers to watch out and to beware, and the command is not limited to the first disciples. The moral is that both an outward religion that is satisfied with appearances and a worldly confidence in power can quietly spread through a community. The description of the disciples' worry about bread is not a command either. It shows what a mind full of a small anxiety does with a large warning.

The refusal of a sign is a statement of Jesus' practice with the Pharisees, not a ban on asking God for guidance or confirmation. Believers can ask God for help and signs of His goodness. What the passage rules out is the demand that God pass a test we have set.

debates.question: Why did Jesus heal the blind man in two stages when He usually healed instantly?

views.label: An enacted parable of the disciples' partial sight
views.case: Placed just before Peter's confession, the gradual healing dramatizes that the disciples, like the man, will first see dimly, that Jesus is the Christ, and then need a further touch to see the cross clearly; the staged miracle is a deliberate object lesson.

views.label: A demonstration that sight is wholly Jesus' gift
views.case: The two touches show the man contributing nothing and depending entirely on Jesus for both the beginning and the completion of his sight, picturing how spiritual understanding is given and perfected by grace alone.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the miracle is a window onto discipleship: seeing Jesus truly is a gift He gives, often in stages, and He does not abandon the half-seeing but completes His work.

debates.question: Why does Jesus refuse to give the Pharisees a sign?

views.label: A sign would not cure unbelief
views.case: Their demand is a test, not a search; hearts set against Him would explain away any sign, as they had already credited His works to the devil, so more evidence would only harden them.

views.label: The decisive sign is reserved for the resurrection
views.case: Jesus withholds a sign on demand because the true authenticating sign of His identity is His death and rising, given in God's time, not a spectacle staged to satisfy sceptics.

debates.bearing: Both hold that faith is not compelled by spectacle; God calls for trust, and the ultimate sign He gives is the cross and empty tomb, not a wonder performed on command.

study.originalLanguages:
Two different words are used for giving thanks over the food, and the difference is easy to miss in English. Over the seven loaves Jesus gave thanks, eucharistesas, verse 6, and over the few small fish He blessed them, eulogesas, verse 7. Both verbs were used for table prayer in Jewish life, the first speaking of gratitude and the second of praise. Eucharistesas is the root of the word Eucharist, and it is the verb used of the cup and the bread at the Last Supper in Luke 22:19 and 1 Corinthians 11:24. Mark's wording therefore shows that the second feeding, like the first, carries the shape of the church's meal.

The word for the baskets is spyris, verse 8, a large basket, as in Acts 9:25, where Paul is lowered over a wall. In the first feeding the baskets were kophinoi. When Jesus reviews the two meals in verses 19 and 20, He preserves the difference. The numbers are exact, twelve and seven, and the disciples answer correctly. Mark does not decode the numbers, and Jesus does not either. He only asks whether they understand.

The refusal of a sign, verse 12, uses a Semitic idiom. The Greek literally says, if a sign shall be given to this generation, and the sentence is left unfinished. It is the form of an oath in Hebrew, which means a strong denial, and so the BSB renders it no sign will be given. Before this, Mark records that Jesus anastenaxas to pneumati, sighed deeply in His spirit. The verb is a strengthened form of the verb of sighing, and the sense is a deep groan. It is the same kind of reaction as the sigh over the deaf man, Mark 7:34, and shows Jesus' grief over unbelief.

The leaven, zyme, is a physical word that carries a moral meaning. In verse 15 Jesus gives it two possessors, the Pharisees and Herod, and Matthew's parallel gives it a different set of possessors, so that Mark's pairing is his own emphasis. The verb for beware is a pair of commands, horate and blepete, both words for seeing: look, watch out. In the context of a chapter about sight, Jesus' warning is a call to see.

In verses 17 and 18 Jesus uses three verbs of perception in quick succession, noeite, syniete and mnemoneuete, which mean to perceive, to understand and to remember. The last is the memory word that runs through Israel's story. The disciples are being asked to do what Israel was told to do, remember what God has done, Deuteronomy 8:2. The phrase their hearts are hard, in verse 17, uses the same verb as Mark 6:52.

The healing of the blind man is full of exact verbs. In verse 24 he anablepsas, looked up, and said he saw people like trees walking. In verse 25 Jesus placed hands on him a second time, and the man diablepsen, looked intently, apekatestē, was restored, and eneblepen telaugos hapanta, saw everything clearly. Apekatestē is a double compound meaning fully restored to a former state, used elsewhere of the withered hand, Mark 3:5. Telaugos carries the sense of seeing clearly from a distance. The last words of Mark's description are almost a definition of the sight that the disciples lack: everything, and clearly, and from far off.

typology.type: Israel's testing of God at Massah and Meribah
typology.fulfillment: At Massah and Meribah the people tested the LORD, asking whether He was among them or not, Exodus 17:7, and later generations were warned against it, Psalm 95:8-9 and Deuteronomy 6:16. The Pharisees do the same thing with Jesus in the same words of testing, demanding a sign from heaven after He has fed thousands. The escalation is that Israel tested God's provision in the wilderness, while the Pharisees test the provider who is standing in front of them. The type is not a perfect match: Israel was thirsty and afraid, while these men were neither, and their testing is a defence of their position, not a cry of need.

At Passover Israel removed leaven from the house as a picture of leaving the old life behind, Exodus 12:15, and Paul reads that ritual as a call to remove malice and wickedness, 1 Corinthians 5:6-8. Jesus warns of a leaven that spreads through a community, hypocrisy and the confidence of worldly power. The escalation is from a seasonal ritual to a daily vigilance. There is also a link in the story: the disciples in the boat have one loaf, and the bread that Jesus has been breaking is the sign of His own body, John 6:51. The type falls short because the Passover leaven was removed once a year, while the heart's leaven needs removing by the gospel.

typology.type: Eyes opened in the age of salvation
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah foretold that the eyes of the blind would be opened, Isaiah 35:5, and that the Servant would open blind eyes and lead the blind by a way they did not know, Isaiah 42:7 and 42:16. The man at Bethsaida is led by the hand along an unfamiliar way, out of the village, and is given sight. In Jesus the promise is carried out in person. The escalation is that physical sight stands for a more important sight, which Jesus later gives His disciples after the resurrection, Luke 24:45. The type is incomplete in this life, because even the healed see partly, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

Some readers see in the two feedings, one among Jews with twelve baskets and one in the Decapolis with seven, a picture of one Lord feeding both peoples from the same loaves. The text itself does not state this, so it is an inference. What it does say is that the same compassion and the same miracle happen on either side of the lake, and Jesus treats them as one lesson, verses 19 to 21. The fulfilment is the one table that Paul describes, where Gentiles share in Israel's blessings and glorify God for His mercy, Romans 15:8-9. The correspondence is held loosely because the numbers are never explained.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through His compassion for people the world overlooked. In the first feeding the crowd were like sheep without a shepherd. Here the crowd have been three days without food, and Jesus speaks of the matter as a burden on Himself: I have compassion for this crowd, they have been with Me three days, they will faint along the way. His worry about their journey home is a shepherd's worry. Mark presents a Lord who counts the days His people have gone without and cares about the road they must travel afterwards.

The refusal of a sign leads to Christ by contrast. The Pharisees want an undeniable demonstration, but Jesus gives them nothing because the thing they ask for is not what they need. The sign of Jonah that Matthew records, Matthew 12:39-40, points to the real sign, His death and rising. Mark does not include that explanation, but he has arranged for the reader to feel its absence: this is the section of the Gospel just before the first prediction of the cross. The only sign that will settle who He is will be given in the tomb and outside it. The generation that wants a spectacle is offered a crucified and risen Lord.

The leaven warning leads to Christ as the true bread. A one-loaf boat is a small picture, and one writer after another has suggested that the one loaf the disciples had with them is Christ Himself, as John 6:51 says, I am the living bread. Mark does not state it, so this is a possibility that a careful reader may entertain, not a certainty. But the point is clear enough without it: the disciples are worrying about bread while the Bread of Life is sitting in their boat.

The healing of the blind man leads to Christ as the one who completes what He begins. He takes the man by the hand and leads him out, and then He acts twice. The Gospel does not suggest that His power fell short at the first attempt. The staging is for the disciples and the reader. The one who opens the eyes of the blind, Psalm 146:8, does so patiently and personally, and He asks a question, can you see anything, that invites the man to say honestly what he sees. The Lord is not offended by an honest report of a blurred view. He asks for it.

Finally, the section leads to Christ as the one who Himself will open the disciples' eyes. After the resurrection, on the road to Emmaus, their eyes were opened and they recognised Him, Luke 24:31, and He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, Luke 24:45. The second touch in Mark 8 is a promise of the second touch that the disciples will receive. The caution is that the staging of the miracle does not mean that the blind man stands for Peter in every detail; the parallel is to the pattern of partial then full sight, which Mark himself sets by placing the miracle where he does.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who is full of compassion for people who are not His covenant people by descent. The crowd in the Decapolis is hungry, and Jesus claims their need as His own. The God of Israel is not narrow. Jonah had to learn that God cares for a great city of people who did not know their right hand from their left, Jonah 4:11, and Mark gives the same lesson in bread.

He is a God who refuses to be tested. The Pharisees' demand puts God in the dock, and Jesus' sigh shows grief, not irritation. Scripture says plainly that God may not be put to the proof, Deuteronomy 6:16, and Psalm 95 says that Israel's fathers tested and tried Him even though they had seen His work. The God of this chapter gives signs in abundance to those who come in need and withholds them from those who come to examine. Seeing His work is not enough; seeing must be joined to trust.

He is a God who knows what His people are discussing. Jesus knew their conversation in the boat and spoke to the real problem beneath it. Their talk was about bread, and His concern was their hearts. The same God who sees the crowd's hunger sees the disciples' confusion, and He speaks to it directly.

He is a God of patience in teaching. Jesus asks question after question, as God asked Job and as He asked Adam in the garden. The questions are designed to bring the disciples to see, not to humiliate them. And when they still do not see, He does not give up. The scene ends, not with an accusation, but with a healing that offers them hope. The doctrine of God that this holds is that He is both holy and patient, one who does not tolerate hardness and one who does not abandon the hard.

He is a God who works in stages. The two-stage healing is a reminder that God does not always work in a single stroke. He did not create the world in a moment, Genesis 1, and He does not sanctify His people in one. His work is complete, but its completion is given over time. This does not mean that He is incapable, only that He has chosen a way of working that involves a relationship, a question and a second touch.

For worship, the passage invites us to bring our blurred sight honestly to Him and to ask for the second touch. It also teaches us to give thanks before the food is multiplied, as Jesus did, rather than after, trusting that the God who feeds Jew and Gentile alike will provide for the journey home.

crossReferences.note: The people asked whether God could prepare a table in the wilderness, even after seeing water gush from the rock. The disciples' question in Mark 8:4, where could anyone find enough bread, repeats the doubt of the psalm, and the repetition shows that a people can see the works of God and still ask the same question.

Israel called the place Massah and Meribah because they tested the LORD by asking whether He was among them or not. The Pharisees' demand for a sign tests the one in whom God is present. The episode explains why Jesus sighs and why He will give no sign to test Him.

Moses commands Israel not to test the LORD as at Massah. Jesus uses this verse against Satan in the wilderness, Matthew 4:7. In Mark 8 the same command stands behind His refusal: those who demand that God prove Himself have already stepped across a line that Scripture drew.

God describes a foolish and senseless people who have eyes and do not see, ears and do not hear. Jesus' questions to the disciples in Mark 8:18 draw on this. The effect is to place the disciples, at least for the moment, in the position of those Jeremiah rebuked, and to warn them.

Isaiah is told to say to the people, be ever hearing but never understanding. Mark has already applied this to those outside, Mark 4:12. Its return in Mark 8 means that the disciples are not exempt, and that the mystery of hardness reaches into the circle of followers.

Leaven was removed from Israelite houses at the Passover. The practice gives the image Jesus uses its force, because a community that had learned to hunt out leaven each year would grasp the danger of a small thing spreading. It also links the warning to the feast of deliverance.

Paul asks whether the Corinthians know that a little leaven works through the whole batch, and tells them to clear out the old leaven because Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. He applies Jesus' image to the life of a congregation and ties it to the cross.

On the day of salvation the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. Mark 7 gave the second half of the promise and Mark 8 gives the first. Taken together the two healings show the age of salvation breaking in through the touch of Jesus.

God promises to lead the blind by a way they did not know and to turn darkness into light before them. The man at Bethsaida is led by the hand along a path he cannot see and ends in the light. The promise ends with the assurance that God will not forsake them, which is the other half of Jesus' second touch.

Bartimaeus, a blind beggar at Jericho, receives his sight and follows Jesus on the road. The story is the partner of Mark 8:22-26, and between them the central section of the Gospel is bracketed by two healings of the blind. By the end of that section, the disciples are meant to have been brought, at least in part, from the first stage to the second.

After the resurrection Jesus opens the minds of the disciples to understand the Scriptures. This is the second touch for which Mark 8 prepares. The sight that the disciples lacked in the boat is given them by the risen Lord who walks with them and explains what the cross meant.

Paul says that now we see only a dim reflection, then face to face. The man who sees trees walking is a picture of our present sight. It is real and still partial, and it will be completed when we see Him as He is. The passage gives believers patience with their own blur.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning of the Bible, seeing and not seeing run through the story. In the garden the first thing the pair did after eating was to see that they were naked, Genesis 3:7, and the sight they gained was a wrong kind of sight. After that God keeps opening eyes: He opens Hagar's eyes to a well, Genesis 21:19, and Elisha's servant's eyes to a hill full of chariots, 2 Kings 6:17. The prophets then describe a people with eyes who cannot see, and promise that one day God will open them.

Mark 8 is where that promise becomes a person. The Lord who made eyes now touches them, and does it in the presence of disciples who have eyes and do not yet see. The section answers a question the Old Testament leaves open, which is how a people who have seen the exodus, the manna, the signs and the wonders can still not know their God. The answer is that seeing is not enough. Sight has to be given, and it is given by Christ.

The passage also gathers the bread thread. In the wilderness God fed Israel with manna, and Israel complained. Jesus feeds Jew and Gentile alike, and the disciples worry about their lack. The bread points ahead to the table where Jesus will say, This is My body, Mark 14:22, and to the one loaf of the church, 1 Corinthians 10:17. The warning about leaven looks forward to the apostles' warnings about false teaching and hypocrisy, and back to the old bread of Egypt.

What the story sets up is Caesarea Philippi, where Peter will see that Jesus is the Christ and not yet see what that means. The two-stage healing is the lens through which the whole next half of Mark is read. After the cross and the empty tomb, the second touch comes, and the apostles can see and preach.

The story ends in a place where nothing is dim. In the new creation God's servants will see His face, Revelation 22:4, and the dim reflection of this life gives way to full knowledge, 1 Corinthians 13:12. The blind receive sight, the hungry are fed and the leaven of the old world is gone. The meal that Jesus prepared on a Decapolis hillside becomes the wedding supper of the Lamb, with guests from every nation, Revelation 19:9.

quiz.q: What is significant about the feeding of the four thousand compared with the five thousand?

options.text: It shows Jesus' compassion and provision reaching into Gentile territory as well as to Israel.
options.note: The four thousand were fed in Gentile country, extending the shepherd-heart of Jesus to the nations.

options.text: It shows Jesus could repeat a miracle He had done before.
options.note: True, but the deeper point is the widening of His provision to Gentiles, not mere repetition.

options.text: It proves the disciples had finally learned to trust Him.
options.note: The opposite; they still asked where bread could be found, showing they had not understood.

options.text: It was only a symbolic story, not a real event.
options.note: Mark presents it as a real feeding with counted loaves, people, and leftovers.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus refuse the Pharisees' demand for a sign?

options.text: Their demand was a test, not a search; no sign would satisfy hearts set against believing.
options.note: Mark 8:11-12; Jesus sighs and refuses, since unbelief would explain away any sign.

options.text: Because He was unable to give them a sign at that moment.
options.note: Jesus was fully able; He chose not to perform on demand.

options.text: Because the true sign of His identity would be His resurrection.
options.note: True, He reserves the decisive sign for the resurrection, but here His stated reason is their testing, unbelieving demand.

options.text: Because signs are always wrong to give.
options.note: Jesus gave many signs; He refused this one because it sprang from a testing heart.

quiz.q: What did Jesus mean by the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod?

options.text: Their corrupting influence, the hypocrisy and unbelief of the Pharisees and the worldly power-seeking of Herod, which spreads quietly like yeast.
options.note: Leaven pictures a pervasive corruption to be guarded against, Mark 8:15.

options.text: A warning about literal bread they had failed to bring.
options.note: The disciples made that mistake; Jesus was speaking of corrupting influence, not bread.

options.text: A caution about the spreading danger of bad teaching and attitudes.
options.note: Close, but it should name the specific corruption of the Pharisees and Herod that Jesus targets.

options.text: A command to avoid all contact with rulers.
options.note: Jesus warns against their corrupting influence, not against all contact with authorities.

quiz.q: Why does Mark record the blind man being healed in two stages just before Peter's confession?

options.text: As a living parable that the disciples, like the man, see Jesus only partly and need a further touch to see clearly.
options.note: The staged healing mirrors Peter's partial sight: right that Jesus is Christ, but not yet seeing the cross.

options.text: To show that Jesus sometimes needed two attempts to heal.
options.note: Jesus was never limited; the two stages are a deliberate object lesson, not a failure.

options.text: To illustrate that spiritual sight is a gift Jesus gives, sometimes gradually.
options.note: True and important, but it should also connect to the disciples' partial understanding that follows.

options.text: Simply because that is the order events happened, with no meaning.
options.note: Mark places the account deliberately as a parable of discipleship, not as a meaningless sequence.

quiz.q: What is the recurring concern Jesus presses on the disciples in this section?

options.text: That they still do not see or understand who He is, despite all they have witnessed.
options.note: Mark 8:17-21; do you still not understand, having eyes but not seeing.

options.text: That they had failed to bring enough bread.
options.note: That was their misunderstanding; Jesus was concerned with their spiritual dullness.

options.text: That they were slow to grasp His identity and mission.
options.note: Correct in substance, but the sharper point is their failure to see and understand despite the evidence.

options.text: That they trusted Him too much.
options.note: The problem was too little understanding and trust, not too much.

questions: Jesus was moved with compassion for a hungry, weary crowd. Where do you need to trust His compassion for you in a place that feels desolate?
The Pharisees wanted a sign on their terms rather than faith. Do you ever demand that God prove Himself your way instead of trusting what He has already shown?
Leaven spreads quietly and corrupts the whole batch. What small, unnoticed influences of hypocrisy or worldliness might be spreading in your heart?
The blind man saw only blurred shapes until Jesus touched him again. In what area do you sense you are seeing only in part and need Jesus to open your eyes further?
Jesus kept asking, do you still not understand? What is He patiently trying to help you see about Himself right now?

translationNotes.note: About four thousand men were present; men is implied, that is, besides women and children, as the parallel in Matthew 15:38 makes explicit.
No sign will be given to this generation renders a strong Hebraic oath form; Jesus firmly refuses a sign on demand, though the parallels add the exception of the sign of Jonah, His resurrection.
Having eyes, do you not see, having ears, do you not hear draws on Jeremiah 5:21 and Ezekiel 12:2, applying the prophets' rebuke of a dull people to the disciples themselves.
